summary: This proposed standard recommends implementation and configuration practices for IKEv2 responders so that they can resist denial-of-service and distributed denial-of-service attacks. It also introduces a mechanism called Client Puzzles that helps defend against such attacks.

plainLanguage.summary: If too many fake visitors crowd the front desk, real ones cannot get in. This gives tips and a small puzzle visitors must solve first, so attackers cannot cheaply swamp the desk.

questions: how to protect ikev2 from ddos
what is a half open ike sa
how hard should an ikev2 puzzle be
subtitle: Defenses and a proof-of-work puzzle that help IKEv2 servers survive floods of fake connection attempts.

tldr.problem: An IKEv2 Responder allocates memory for a half-open security association after one cheap IKE_SA_INIT request, so botnets can exhaust its memory or CPU, and the existing cookie only stops spoofed addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends shorter retention, per-address or per-prefix rate limits, cookies and a staged defense plan. It adds client puzzles: the Initiator must find four keys whose PRF output over the cookie ends in enough zero bits.
tldr.outcome: Responders get a way to make each half-open SA costlier for attackers. The RFC notes puzzles only become a really powerful defense once most legitimate clients support them.

today: RFC 8019 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the cookie mechanism in RFC 7296.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Denial-of-service attacks are hard to defend against because a victim's resources are bounded, and some resources are needed just to tell a real session from an attack. The Internet Key Exchange Protocol version 2 (IKEv2, RFC 7296) already has a cookie mechanism that protects a Responder from attacks using spoofed IP addresses.

Botnets, however, make distributed attacks (DDoS) possible, and these are harder to stop. RFC 8019 gives recommendations that help a Responder resist DoS and DDoS attacks, and it introduces a new mechanism, puzzles.
sections.plainLanguage: There was already a basic guard at the door, but a big crowd of real-looking troublemakers can still get through. This document adds more guards and a puzzle to slow the crowd down.

sections.title: The Vulnerability
sections.content:
In the IKE_SA_INIT exchange the Initiator sends one message. The Responder replies and also allocates memory for a half-open IKE SA, which is later authenticated in IKE_AUTH. If no IKE_AUTH request arrives, the half-open SA is kept for an unspecified time. Depending on algorithms and implementation, it uses from around one hundred to several thousand bytes.

Making IKE_SA_INIT requests is cheap, so flooding a Responder is an easy way to use up its resources. The Responder faces three stages of work. Stage 1 (IKE_SA_INIT) is light on CPU but needs storage. Stage 2 (IKE_AUTH) needs private-key operations and is much heavier. Stage 3 may involve public key operations if certificates are present. Attackers who cannot authenticate never reach the fourth stage, creating the Child SA.

Shortening retention time helps. For example, with a capacity of 60,000 half-open SAs, a 1-minute retention means an attacker needs 1,000 half-open SAs per second, while a 3-second retention means 20,000 per second. Attackers can also skip memory exhaustion and send junk IKE_AUTH requests, which force the Responder to derive keys only to fail the integrity check.

The RFC says a defense strategy needs at least four components: shorter half-open retention, rate limiting by address or prefix, guidance for failed IKE_AUTH decryption, and raising the cost of half-open SAs up to what legitimate clients tolerate. Puzzles serve the fourth.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening a file for each visitor costs the desk a little, but pretending to be a visitor costs a faker almost nothing. Enough fakers fill every drawer.

sections.title: Defenses While the IKE SA Is Created
sections.content:
Retention. When not under attack, the half-open SA timeout SHOULD be high enough for several retransmissions. Under attack it can be cut, but the Responder must still allow for the round trip and the Initiator's key derivation. Two seconds is probably as low as can realistically be used.

Rate limiting. Limit concurrent half-open SAs per address (IPv4) or per /48 or /64 prefix (IPv6). A hard limit rejects further IKE_SA_INIT requests, which caps the attacker but lets one bad customer block a whole NAT address. A soft limit requires a puzzle past the threshold, so legitimate clients can still connect, but an attacker with enough CPU can still cause trouble.

Cookies. The stateless cookie of RFC 7296 stops spoofed sources because the attacker needs a routable address to return it. Botnets with real addresses can still fill the table, with state that can reach hundreds of megabytes.

Other measures. Prefer peers presenting Session Resumption tickets (RFC 5723) without serving only them. Keep computed SK_* keys after a failed IKE_AUTH so the attack cannot be repeated on one SA. For the Hash and URL certificate encoding, read the ASN.1 length first, sanity-check it, apply a hard limit on bytes fetched, and let administrators disable the feature or restrict it to trusted URLs. Fragmentation attacks are covered in RFC 7383.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk can forget unfinished visitors sooner, limit how many forms one street can start, and ask each visitor to prove their address by sending back a ticket.

sections.title: How a Puzzle Works
sections.content:
A puzzle extends the cookie mechanism and is loosely based on proof-of-work. It caps how many negotiations an attacker can start per unit time, based on the attacker's CPU. The Responder sends a puzzle when it is too overloaded to create half-open SAs without one, or when rate limiting requires one for a given address or prefix.

The challenge has three parts: the cookie, the identifier of a PRF algorithm chosen from those the Initiator offered, and the Zero-Bit Count (ZBC), the required run of zero bits at the end of the PRF output. The ZBC is a number between 8 and 255, or the special value 0 meaning the Initiator picks its own effort.

The Initiator tries different keys and must return four keys such that PRF(key, cookie) has enough trailing zero bits for each. Using several keys reduces the variance in solving time. The Responder checks that the cookie is valid and that all four results have the required zeros.

In IKE_AUTH the string being hashed differs: it is the Responder nonce Nr joined with the Responder SPI, and the ZBC must not be 0.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor must find four lucky numbers that make a scrambling machine give an answer ending in lots of zeros. Finding them takes real effort, but checking them is quick.

sections.title: Using Puzzles in IKEv2
sections.content:
In IKE_SA_INIT, a Responder under attack first asks for a cookie when the volume is moderate and for a puzzle when it is high. A puzzle response carries both a COOKIE and a PUZZLE notification; PUZZLE MUST always come with COOKIE. An Initiator that does not support puzzles, or will not pay, ignores the PUZZLE notification and repeats the request with the cookie. A supporting Initiator solves it and adds a Puzzle Solution (PS) payload.

The Responder looks at the repeated request. A request without a solved puzzle gets the lowest priority. A request with a solution gets higher priority for more zero bits, more consecutive puzzles solved, and more time spent. The Responder may accept it, reject it, or hand out a new puzzle. It MAY also serve a fraction of legacy requests at random, but only those that carry a valid cookie.

Difficulty 0 lets the Initiator spend as much effort as it can afford, and the RFC recommends this in diverse environments unless the attack volume is very high. The cookie SHOULD let the Responder learn whether a puzzle was given, its difficulty, how many puzzles in a row, and how long solving took; if that data is encoded in the cookie it MUST be integrity protected, and cookies cannot exceed 64 bytes.

In IKE_AUTH, the Responder can add a puzzle only if one was presented and solved in IKE_SA_INIT. The Initiator puts the PS payload outside the Encrypted payload, so the Responder can check it before computing the DH shared secret and keys. Without a valid PS payload, the Responder MUST silently discard the request, and it MUST verify all four keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The desk hands out a puzzle with the ticket. Visitors who solve it get in first, and visitors who skip it wait at the back of the line.

sections.title: PUZZLE Notification and PS Payload
sections.content:
The PUZZLE notification has Protocol ID 0, SPI Size 0 and Notify Message Type 16434. It then carries a 2-octet PRF Transform ID that MUST be used for the puzzle and a 1-octet Difficulty giving the minimum trailing zero bits. It contains no data.

The Puzzle Solution (PS) payload is payload type 54. Its data is four different keys for the selected PRF, all the same size, and must not be empty. Each key is between 1 octet and the PRF's preferred key length when the PRF accepts any size, and the RFC expects keys of 4 octets or fewer in most cases. The Responder finds the key size by dividing the data size by 4.
sections.plainLanguage: The puzzle note says which scrambler to use and how many zeros to find. The answer sheet holds the four lucky numbers.

sections.title: Defense Plan and Tuning
sections.content:
The plan is staged, and the numbers are illustrative, not normative. Countermeasures cost legitimate Initiators effort, so they SHOULD NOT run unless an attack is likely. With no attack, use no cookies or puzzles and a soft limit of 3 to 5 half-open SAs per address or prefix. When an attack is seen, first require stateless cookies from everyone. If that is not enough, use puzzles or harder puzzles for suspicious nodes, then hard limits, and finally a puzzle for all Initiators, which is the last resort.

Detection is workload-specific. The example Responder with 10,000 peers treats 100 concurrent half-open SAs as a sign of attack. After the IKE SA exists, abusive peers (especially NULL-authenticated ones) can be handled by keeping the IKEv2 window size at one, replying TEMPORARY_FAILURE, adding a short delay, or deleting the SA.

For difficulty, the RFC suggests about 1 second of solving time. It calls 20 zero bits a good compromise at the time of writing, while noting that phones are considerably weaker, and says Initiators SHOULD set a maximum difficulty they will attempt. Parameters SHOULD be tunable, if only so protection can be turned off for benchmarking.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not make everyone solve puzzles on a quiet day. Start with small steps, and use the hardest puzzle only when the crowd will not go away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Difficulty has to be balanced. Puzzles that are too easy for attackers only burden legitimate users, and puzzles that are too hard cause unacceptable delay and battery drain for them, which also counts as a successful attack. The RFC recommends tuning difficulty so the Responder's load stays close to the maximum it can tolerate, adjusted dynamically.

If the cookie is made as in RFC 7296, an attacker can reuse the same SPIi and Ni so the same cookie, and therefore a puzzle solution, can be reused for free. Implementations MUST counter this, for example by changing the cookie secret often, or by adding a timestamp or global counter to the cookie. IKE_AUTH puzzles do not have this problem if SPIr and Nr are random.

The RFC also notes that NULL Authentication leaves peers anonymous after the IKE SA exists, and that implementations must follow the retransmission rules of RFC 7296 to prevent amplification attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: A puzzle that is too easy stops nobody, and one that is too hard stops everyone. Also, the desk must not hand out the same puzzle twice, or a faker can copy an old answer.
